title: SaaS Backup & Disaster Recovery: RPO, RTO and PITR
summary:
A nightly pg_dump to the same VPS is not a backup strategy. It is a file that disappears with the disk, the compromised root account or the provider incident that took the server down in the first place, and even when it survives it can only take you back to 2 AM. For a SaaS product, the real questions are how much data you can afford to lose (RPO), how long you can afford to be down (RTO), and whether anyone has actually restored from your backups recently.

At Loop Origin we run Laravel and Node SaaS platforms on VPS infrastructure for clients, and backup design is part of every server setup and maintenance engagement. This is the setup I deploy by default, with the configuration, restore commands and drill schedule.

What is a good backup and disaster recovery setup for a SaaS on a VPS?

Direct answer: Combine continuous database archiving for point-in-time recovery (PostgreSQL WAL with pgBackRest or WAL-G, MySQL binary logs) with periodic full backups pushed to versioned, write-protected object storage in a separate account and region. Define RPO and RTO per tier, encrypt everything, and run a timed restore drill every month.

RPO and RTO tiers: pick one per system, not per company

RPO (recovery point objective) is how much recent data you can lose. RTO (recovery time objective) is how long recovery may take. They drive cost, so set them per system rather than declaring "zero data loss" for everything.

Tier Typical RPO Typical RTO Mechanism Fits
Tier 0 Seconds Minutes Streaming replica plus WAL/binlog archiving, scripted failover Payments, orders, core tenant data
Tier 1 Minutes 1-4 hours Continuous WAL/binlog archive plus daily full backup, restore to new VPS Most B2B SaaS primary databases
Tier 2 24 hours 1 day Nightly full backup to object storage Analytics copies, internal tools
Tier 3 Rebuildable Days Infrastructure as code, no data backup Caches, queues, search indexes rebuilt from source

Most clients I work with land on Tier 1 for the primary database and Tier 2 or 3 for everything else. Redis queues and Elasticsearch-style indexes are usually Tier 3: rebuild them from the database instead of backing them up. My guide on running Laravel queues in production covers why failed jobs should live in the database rather than only in Redis.

Why dumps alone are not enough

A logical dump (pg_dump, mysqldump) is a consistent snapshot at one moment. If a bad migration or an accidental DELETE without a WHERE runs at 4:40 PM, a nightly dump takes you back to the previous night and you lose the day. Point-in-time recovery (PITR) closes that gap: restore the last full physical backup, then replay the database's change log up to the second before the mistake.

Dumps are still useful for moving individual tenants, seeding staging and long-term archives. They are just not the recovery mechanism for the primary.

PostgreSQL PITR with pgBackRest

postgresql.conf changes (restart required for archive_mode and wal_level):

wal_level = replica
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=main archive-push %p'
archive_timeout = 60          # force a WAL segment switch at least every 60s

/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf:

[global]
repo1-type=s3
repo1-s3-bucket=acme-db-backups
repo1-s3-endpoint=s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com
repo1-s3-region=eu-central-1
repo1-path=/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-full=4
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-cipher-pass=
compress-type=zst
start-fast=y

[main]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/16/main

Initialize, verify and schedule:

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main stanza-create
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main check          # confirms WAL archiving works
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main --type=full backup   # weekly via cron/systemd timer
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main --type=diff backup   # daily
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main info

archive_timeout = 60 is what makes the RPO roughly one minute on a quiet database: without it, a low-traffic system may not fill and ship a 16 MB WAL segment for a long time.

The restore you will run when someone drops a table at 16:40:

sudo systemctl stop postgresql
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main --delta \
  --type=time --target="2026-10-31 16:39:00+05" --target-action=promote restore
sudo systemctl start postgresql

In practice I restore to a new server first, verify the data, then cut over or copy the missing rows back. Restoring over the only production copy removes your ability to try again.

WAL-G is the main alternative: archive_command = 'wal-g wal-push %p', wal-g backup-push $PGDATA for base backups, and wal-g backup-fetch $PGDATA LATEST plus restore_command = 'wal-g wal-fetch %f %p' and recovery_target_time for PITR. I prefer pgBackRest for its built-in check, retention and parallel restore, and WAL-G where a team already uses it.

MySQL and MariaDB PITR with binary logs 

# my.cnf
[mysqld]
server_id = 1
log_bin = /var/lib/mysql/binlog
binlog_format = ROW
binlog_expire_logs_seconds = 1209600   # 14 days, longer than your full-backup interval
sync_binlog = 1

Take a consistent full backup with Percona XtraBackup for large databases, or mysqldump --single-transaction --source-data=2 for smaller ones (--source-data replaced --master-data in MySQL 8.0.26). Ship binlogs off the server continuously, for example with mysqlbinlog --read-from-remote-server --raw --stop-never running on a backup host.

Recovery: restore the full backup, read the binlog file and position recorded in it, then replay up to just before the incident:

mysqlbinlog --start-position=157 --stop-datetime="2026-10-31 16:39:00" \
  binlog.000412 binlog.000413 | mysql -u root -p

--stop-datetime is interpreted in the local time zone of the machine running mysqlbinlog, a detail that has caught more than one team restoring on a UTC server.

Object storage: where backups survive the incident

The repository must survive the loss of the server and of the credentials on it:

  • Separate account or project for the backup bucket, with a write-only key on the server. A stolen server key should not be able to delete backups.
  • Versioning plus object lock (S3 Object Lock, or the equivalent on S3-compatible providers that support it) with a retention period longer than your detection window.
  • A different region or provider from the primary VPS.
  • Client-side encryption (pgBackRest's repo1-cipher-type, or restic for file backups) with the passphrase stored outside the server.
  • File uploads (storage/app, user uploads) backed up with restic or rclone, or written directly to object storage in the first place.

Cost drivers, compared

Component What drives cost How to control it
Object storage Total stored size × retention Compression (zstd), differential backups, retention limits
Request and egress fees Restore downloads, frequent small uploads Choose providers with low egress; restore drills to the same region
Standby replica (Tier 0) A second always-on server Use only for systems that truly need minute-level RTO
Restore drill servers Hours of a temporary VPS per month Script the drill, destroy the server afterwards
Engineer time Setup, monitoring, drills Automate checks and alerts; document the runbook

For most Tier 1 SaaS databases the storage bill is small next to the replica and engineering time. My VPS vs managed PaaS cost comparison shows where managed databases with built-in PITR change the calculation.

Failure modes I have seen

  • Archiving silently broken. archive_command fails, WAL piles up in pg_wal and the disk fills. Monitor pg_stat_archiver.failed_count and the age of last_archived_time.
  • Backups nobody restored. Encryption passphrase lost, wrong PostgreSQL major version, missing extensions. Only a drill finds these.
  • Same blast radius. Backups in a bucket the compromised server can delete.
  • Binlog retention shorter than the backup interval. A gap makes PITR impossible past the last full backup.
  • Forgotten tenants' files. The database restores, but uploaded documents do not.
  • Shared-database multi-tenancy surprises. Restoring one tenant from a shared physical backup needs a side restore and a selective copy; plan it. My multi-tenant SaaS database architecture guide covers the trade-offs.

Monthly restore drill runbook

  1. Provision a clean VPS from infrastructure code.
  2. Restore the latest full backup plus WAL or binlogs to a target time from yesterday.
  3. Time it end to end; compare against your RTO.
  4. Run integrity checks: row counts on key tables, latest order or invoice timestamp, application smoke test.
  5. Restore a sample of uploaded files and open them.
  6. Record duration, issues and the backup set used in the runbook.
  7. Destroy the drill server and rotate any credentials it used.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between RPO and RTO?

RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time between the last recoverable point and the incident. RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service. A system can have a one-minute RPO and a four-hour RTO, and the two are engineered with different tools.

Is pg_dump enough for a production SaaS database?

Not as the only mechanism. It restores to the moment the dump ran, so anything after that is lost. Use physical backups with WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery, and keep logical dumps for tenant exports, staging data and long-term archives.

pgBackRest or WAL-G?

Both provide base backups, WAL archiving to object storage, compression, encryption and PITR. pgBackRest has a built-in configuration check, retention management and parallel restore. WAL-G is lighter and common in container setups. Choose the one your team will monitor and drill.

How often should I test restoring backups?

At least monthly for production databases, and after any major version upgrade, storage change or backup configuration change. A drill should restore to a fresh server, be timed against your RTO and include an application-level check, not just a successful exit code.

Should backups be stored in the same cloud provider?

A different region at minimum, and ideally a separate account with write-only credentials from the server and object lock enabled. A different provider adds protection against account-level incidents at the cost of egress fees during restores.

Do I need to back up Redis?

Usually not, if Redis holds caches, sessions and queues that can be rebuilt or retried. Keep durable state such as failed jobs and anything business-critical in the main database. Back up Redis only if it is your primary store for data you cannot regenerate.

Redis queues and Elasticsearch-style indexes are usually Tier 3: rebuild them from the database instead of backing them up. My guide on running Laravel queues in production covers why failed jobs should live in the database rather than only in Redis.

Why dumps alone are not enough

A logical dump (pg_dump, mysqldump) is a consistent snapshot at one moment. If a bad migration or an accidental DELETE without a WHERE runs at 4:40 PM, a nightly dump takes you back to the previous night and you lose the day. Point-in-time recovery (PITR) closes that gap: restore the last full physical backup, then replay the database's change log up to the second before the mistake.

Dumps are still useful for moving individual tenants, seeding staging and long-term archives. They are just not the recovery mechanism for the primary.

PostgreSQL PITR with pgBackRest

postgresql.conf changes (restart required for archive_mode and wal_level):

wal_level = replica
archive_mode = on
archive_command = 'pgbackrest --stanza=main archive-push %p'
archive_timeout = 60          # force a WAL segment switch at least every 60s

/etc/pgbackrest/pgbackrest.conf:

[global]
repo1-type=s3
repo1-s3-bucket=acme-db-backups
repo1-s3-endpoint=s3.eu-central-1.amazonaws.com
repo1-s3-region=eu-central-1
repo1-path=/pgbackrest
repo1-retention-full=4
repo1-cipher-type=aes-256-cbc
repo1-cipher-pass=
compress-type=zst
start-fast=y

[main]
pg1-path=/var/lib/postgresql/16/main

Initialize, verify and schedule:

sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main stanza-create
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main check          # confirms WAL archiving works
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main --type=full backup   # weekly via cron/systemd timer
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main --type=diff backup   # daily
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main info

archive_timeout = 60 is what makes the RPO roughly one minute on a quiet database: without it, a low-traffic system may not fill and ship a 16 MB WAL segment for a long time.

The restore you will run when someone drops a table at 16:40:

sudo systemctl stop postgresql
sudo -u postgres pgbackrest --stanza=main --delta \
  --type=time --target="2026-10-31 16:39:00+05" --target-action=promote restore
sudo systemctl start postgresql

In practice I restore to a new server first, verify the data, then cut over or copy the missing rows back. Restoring over the only production copy removes your ability to try again.

WAL-G is the main alternative: archive_command = 'wal-g wal-push %p', wal-g backup-push $PGDATA for base backups, and wal-g backup-fetch $PGDATA LATEST plus restore_command = 'wal-g wal-fetch %f %p' and recovery_target_time for PITR. I prefer pgBackRest for its built-in check, retention and parallel restore, and WAL-G where a team already uses it.

MySQL and MariaDB PITR with binary logs 

# my.cnf
[mysqld]
server_id = 1
log_bin = /var/lib/mysql/binlog
binlog_format = ROW
binlog_expire_logs_seconds = 1209600   # 14 days, longer than your full-backup interval
sync_binlog = 1

Take a consistent full backup with Percona XtraBackup for large databases, or mysqldump --single-transaction --source-data=2 for smaller ones (--source-data replaced --master-data in MySQL 8.0.26). Ship binlogs off the server continuously, for example with mysqlbinlog --read-from-remote-server --raw --stop-never running on a backup host.

Recovery: restore the full backup, read the binlog file and position recorded in it, then replay up to just before the incident:

mysqlbinlog --start-position=157 --stop-datetime="2026-10-31 16:39:00" \
  binlog.000412 binlog.000413 | mysql -u root -p

--stop-datetime is interpreted in the local time zone of the machine running mysqlbinlog, a detail that has caught more than one team restoring on a UTC server.

Object storage: where backups survive the incident

The repository must survive the loss of the server and of the credentials on it:

  • Separate account or project for the backup bucket, with a write-only key on the server. A stolen server key should not be able to delete backups.
  • Versioning plus object lock (S3 Object Lock, or the equivalent on S3-compatible providers that support it) with a retention period longer than your detection window.
  • A different region or provider from the primary VPS.
  • Client-side encryption (pgBackRest's repo1-cipher-type, or restic for file backups) with the passphrase stored outside the server.
  • File uploads (storage/app, user uploads) backed up with restic or rclone, or written directly to object storage in the first place.

Cost drivers, compared

Component What drives cost How to control it
Object storage Total stored size × retention Compression (zstd), differential backups, retention limits
Request and egress fees Restore downloads, frequent small uploads Choose providers with low egress; restore drills to the same region
Standby replica (Tier 0) A second always-on server Use only for systems that truly need minute-level RTO
Restore drill servers Hours of a temporary VPS per month Script the drill, destroy the server afterwards
Engineer time Setup, monitoring, drills Automate checks and alerts; document the runbook

For most Tier 1 SaaS databases the storage bill is small next to the replica and engineering time. My VPS vs managed PaaS cost comparison shows where managed databases with built-in PITR change the calculation.

Failure modes I have seen

  • Archiving silently broken. archive_command fails, WAL piles up in pg_wal and the disk fills. Monitor pg_stat_archiver.failed_count and the age of last_archived_time.
  • Backups nobody restored. Encryption passphrase lost, wrong PostgreSQL major version, missing extensions. Only a drill finds these.
  • Same blast radius. Backups in a bucket the compromised server can delete.
  • Binlog retention shorter than the backup interval. A gap makes PITR impossible past the last full backup.
  • Forgotten tenants' files. The database restores, but uploaded documents do not.
  • Shared-database multi-tenancy surprises. Restoring one tenant from a shared physical backup needs a side restore and a selective copy; plan it. My multi-tenant SaaS database architecture guide covers the trade-offs.

Monthly restore drill runbook

  1. Provision a clean VPS from infrastructure code.
  2. Restore the latest full backup plus WAL or binlogs to a target time from yesterday.
  3. Time it end to end; compare against your RTO.
  4. Run integrity checks: row counts on key tables, latest order or invoice timestamp, application smoke test.
  5. Restore a sample of uploaded files and open them.
  6. Record duration, issues and the backup set used in the runbook.
  7. Destroy the drill server and rotate any credentials it used.

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between RPO and RTO?

RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss, measured as time between the last recoverable point and the incident. RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service. A system can have a one-minute RPO and a four-hour RTO, and the two are engineered with different tools.

Is pg_dump enough for a production SaaS database?

Not as the only mechanism. It restores to the moment the dump ran, so anything after that is lost. Use physical backups with WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery, and keep logical dumps for tenant exports, staging data and long-term archives.

pgBackRest or WAL-G?

Both provide base backups, WAL archiving to object storage, compression, encryption and PITR. pgBackRest has a built-in configuration check, retention management and parallel restore. WAL-G is lighter and common in container setups. Choose the one your team will monitor and drill.

How often should I test restoring backups?

At least monthly for production databases, and after any major version upgrade, storage change or backup configuration change. A drill should restore to a fresh server, be timed against your RTO and include an application-level check, not just a successful exit code.

Should backups be stored in the same cloud provider?

A different region at minimum, and ideally a separate account with write-only credentials from the server and object lock enabled. A different provider adds protection against account-level incidents at the cost of egress fees during restores.

Do I need to back up Redis?

Usually not, if Redis holds caches, sessions and queues that can be rebuilt or retried. Keep durable state such as failed jobs and anything business-critical in the main database. Back up Redis only if it is your primary store for data you cannot regenerate.

title: Your agent's log has 1,509 rows and zero denials. That is the problem.
summary:
An agent that never refuses anything is not a working agent. It is a script with a credit card.

I keep seeing the same artefact offered as proof of control: a log where every row says allowed. Fifteen hundred rows, zero denials, exported to CSV for the auditor. It proves traffic. It does not prove that anything was ever stopped.

What a refusal actually looks like

A deny record is small and boring on purpose:

{
  "v": 1,
  "prev": "",
  "ts": "2026-10-31T09:14:02+00:00",
  "decision": "deny",
  "policy": "spend_limit_per_call",
  "requested": {"amount_usdc": 40},
  "limit": {"amount_usdc": 5},
  "subject": "agent:invoice-runner",
  "signature": "ed25519:..."
}

Four properties make it evidence rather than a note:

  1. It exists only when something was refused. If the file is empty, either nothing was stopped or nothing was checked. Both are answers.
  2. It chains. prev binds each record to the one before it; deleting a row breaks every row after it.
  3. It is signed offline. A verifier checks the chain and the signature without trusting the service that produced it.
  4. It names the policy and the numbers. "Denied" is an opinion; "asked 40, limit 5, policy spend_limit_per_call" is a fact.

The question that breaks most demos

Show me one refusal from last week, with the policy that fired.

Most systems cannot answer it, because denials are logged at the same level as successes and thrown away first.

What this is not

It is not a compliance certificate, and it does not make an agent safe. It makes one narrow claim verifiable: this action was stopped, at this time, under this policy, and the record has not been edited since. Everything else still needs a human.

If you already keep such a log, the only thing I would ask: can someone verify it without your dashboard? If yes, you are ahead of most teams shipping agents today.

I build attest, a deterministic verifier for agent artefacts — schema, emptiness, provenance, and mandate authority, one Ed25519-signed verdict. The deny log is public: https://attest.rta.lat/deny-evidence

title: Run your own model endpoint on a rented GPU with vLLM: your own API key, an SSH tunnel, and an optional LoRA adapter
summary:
Short answer: rent a GPU with SSH access, install vLLM in a fresh Python environment, start it so it listens only on the instance's own localhost, require an API key of your own, and reach it from your machine through an SSH tunnel. If you have a LoRA adapter for the same base model, vLLM can serve it next to the base model under its own name. When you are done, copy out what you need and destroy the instance.

Disclosure: I work on CloudGPU, and the GPU rental in this guide is ours. Each step ends with a "What to check" line, because versions, flags and defaults change.

Which kind of endpoint is this?

CloudGPU's terms (section 6) say that each running instance with a service URL gets a public HTTPS address; these URLs are "hard to guess but they are not authenticated by default", and if you need authentication you configure it inside your instance, for example an API key on your Ollama deployment. The docs say that templates that serve an API, such as Ollama and ComfyUI, get such a URL.

This guide takes a different route on purpose. You rent a raw GPU, run vLLM on it, and do not publish any URL: the server listens only on the instance's own localhost, requires your own API key, and you reach it through an SSH tunnel from your machine. That gives you an endpoint only you can use, as long as you keep the SSH access and the key to yourself.

vLLM's own security guide is clear about the limits of the key: --api-key protects only the endpoints under the /v1, /v2, /inference and /cohere prefixes, other endpoints on the same server are not covered, and it says not to rely on --api-key alone. It also notes that some underlying components may listen on all network interfaces. So treat the key as one layer, keep the tunnel as the way in, and do not send anything to the instance that you would not put on a rented machine.

Read these things first

  1. The license of your base model. An adapter sits on top of a base model, so the base model's license applies to what you serve. The walkthrough uses Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3, whose model card lists the Apache-2.0 license (read 2026-10-27). If you use a small Llama or Gemma model instead, read the Llama 3.2 Community License or the Gemma Terms of Use first, including what they say about derivative models. This guide gives no legal conclusions.
  2. What your adapter was trained on. Use only data you have the right to use; CloudGPU's acceptable use policy (section 1.8) prohibits training on datasets you do not have rights to use. If your adapter was trained on text generated through DeepSeek's API and you publish its outputs, DeepSeek's Terms of Use (Last Update: March 27, 2026) require you to label published outputs as AI-generated (section 3.1).
  3. CloudGPU's terms. Read the terms before you rent. Section 1 says compute comes from third-party data centres and supplier networks, which can change, so this guide does not claim your data stays on any particular machine.

What you need

  • A CloudGPU account with balance. GPU instances are billed per minute, rounded up, with a 1-minute minimum, and billing stops when you destroy the instance (terms). Rates are on the pricing page. Payment is by card or USDT (payments).
  • A terminal with ssh, scp and Python 3 on your own machine.
  • Optional: a LoRA adapter trained on Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3, stored in the usual Hugging Face PEFT layout (a folder with adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors), for example the one from the self-critique guide in this series. Without an adapter, do everything below and skip the adapter parts; you will serve the base model only.

What to check: ssh -V prints a version, and python3 --version prints a version. If you have an adapter, its folder contains the two files above.

Step 1: make your endpoint key and look at your adapter (on your own machine)

The key is a long random string that only you and the server know. Generate one:

python3 -c "import secrets; print(secrets.token_urlsafe(32))"

Keep it in a password manager. Make a new one for every instance; never reuse a key from another service.

If you have an adapter, open adapter_config.json in its folder and note two fields: base_model_name_or_path and r (the LoRA rank).

What to check: the command printed a long random string that you have stored somewhere other than a shell history you share. For an adapter, base_model_name_or_path is mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (if not, the adapter belongs to another base model and this guide's command will not match it), and r is a number you can compare with the rank limit in Step 4.

Step 2: rent a raw GPU

On Deploy, choose Raw GPU and a card. The CloudGPU docs say that every template is a ready-made image with root SSH and that for anything a template does not cover you rent a raw GPU (Deploy â†’ Raw GPU) and install what you need over SSH. The docs' GPU table lists 16 GB as the minimum VRAM for models from 0.5B to 8B parameters; vLLM also needs Linux and an NVIDIA GPU with compute capability 7.5 or higher, according to its installation page. A 7B model in 16-bit needs memory for the weights plus a cache for requests, so a card with more than the minimum is the easy fix if the server reports it cannot fit.

Connect with the SSH details of your running instance. If you have an adapter, upload its folder from your own machine (scp takes the port with a capital -P):

scp -r -P  ./adapter-selfloop @:/workspace/

What to check: ssh -p @ connects, nvidia-smi lists a GPU, and (with an adapter) ls /workspace/adapter-selfloop shows adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors.

Step 3: install vLLM in a fresh environment

The vLLM installation page recommends uv for the Python environment. uv can be installed from PyPI (see the uv installation page). On the instance:

pip install uv
cd /workspace
uv venv --python 3.12 --seed --managed-python
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto

These lines follow the vLLM page as read on 2026-10-27; if the page now shows different commands, use its commands.

What to check: with the environment active, vllm --version prints a version, and python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())" prints True. If the install stops with an error, read the error text and the troubleshooting parts of the vLLM page.

Step 4: start the server on localhost, with your key

Use your own key in place of . With an adapter:

cd /workspace && source .venv/bin/activate
nohup vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --api-key  \
  --tokenizer-mode hf \
  --enable-lora --max-lora-rank 16 \
  --lora-modules selfloop=/workspace/adapter-selfloop \
  > /workspace/vllm.log 2>&1 &

Without an adapter, remove the --enable-lora, --max-lora-rank and --lora-modules lines.

What the flags do, from the vLLM serve reference and LoRA page: --host 127.0.0.1 keeps the HTTP server on the instance's localhost; --api-key makes requests under /v1 carry that key; --tokenizer-mode hf uses the Hugging Face tokenizer instead of letting auto pick the mistral_common tokenizer for Mistral models; pinning it is meant to match how an adapter was trained with the Hugging Face tokenizer, so drop the flag if your adapter was trained another way; --lora-modules name=path registers the adapter under the name selfloop; --max-lora-rank must be at least the adapter's r and the docs list the allowed values (the default is 16), so if your r from Step 1 is larger than 16, use the next allowed value. The key is visible in the instance's process list while the server runs, which is one more reason to use a fresh key per instance.

Wait until the log says the server is ready before you send a request. If the process exits, read the end of the log with tail -n 50 /workspace/vllm.log. A message about memory for the cache is fixed by adding --max-model-len 8192 or by choosing a card with more memory.

What to check: on the instance, curl -s -i http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models | head -n 1 prints an HTTP status line that is not a success (an authentication error is expected, because you sent no key), and curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer " http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models prints JSON that lists the base model and, with an adapter, selfloop.

Step 5: open the tunnel and call your endpoint (on your own machine)

In one terminal, open the tunnel. Nothing is printed while it runs; leave it open:

ssh -N -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 -p  @

If local port 8000 is already used, pick another local port (for example -L 8001:127.0.0.1:8000) and use it in the URLs below. In a second terminal:

curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1/models -H "Authorization: Bearer "

Now the same request through the OpenAI SDK (pip install openai on your own machine). Put this in a file named ask.py:

import os
import sys

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1", api_key=os.environ["ENDPOINT_KEY"])

BASE = "mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3"
ADAPTER = "selfloop"  # delete this name from the loop below if you started without an adapter

question = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "Explain what a LoRA adapter is in two sentences."

for name in (BASE, ADAPTER):
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=name,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
        temperature=0,
        max_tokens=300,
    )
    print("==", name)
    print(reply.choices[0].message.content)
    print()

Run it with the key in an environment variable, not in the file:

export ENDPOINT_KEY=""
python3 ask.py "Explain what a LoRA adapter is in two sentences."

Any tool that lets you set an OpenAI-compatible base URL and a key can use the same two values (http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 and your key) while the tunnel is open.

What to check: the curl call lists the model names you expect; ask.py prints one answer per model name; and a call with a wrong or missing key is refused rather than answered. If the tunnel command prints "address already in use", use another local port. Reading two answers is not a test of your adapter; for that, use questions the adapter never saw and compare them yourself, as in the self-critique guide.

Step 6: stop, copy out what you need, destroy

Close the tunnel with Ctrl+C in its terminal. Before you destroy anything, copy what you want to keep. The docs have a section called "What to save before you destroy an instance"; read it in the CloudGPU docs. For example, copy the server log from your own machine:

scp -P  @:/workspace/vllm.log ./

Then destroy the instance from your Dashboard (the docs: "You can destroy an instance at any time"). Minutes spent copying are billed like any other minute, and billing stops once the instance is destroyed. The endpoint key was meant for this instance only; do not reuse it.

What to check: the instance no longer appears as running in your Dashboard, and the curl call from Step 5 now fails to connect.

Privacy and access, in plain terms

  • This is your own endpoint, with your own API key, reached through your own SSH tunnel. It is not a public URL.
  • Per CloudGPU's terms (section 5), you keep ownership of any data, models, code or output you create on or upload to an instance, and CloudGPU says it does not access, inspect, copy or back up the contents of your instance except in three listed cases: a credible report of a violation of section 3, valid legal process, or to protect the safety of users or third parties.
  • Per the same terms, destroying an instance permanently deletes its local storage, and you are responsible for backing up what you want to keep.
  • Whatever you send to the endpoint is processed on that rented instance. Do not send secrets or personal data you would not put on a rented machine.
  • If you call a model through CloudGPU's AI API instead of your own instance, the request is forwarded to the model provider and its terms apply; see the privacy policy.

Sources

All read on 2026-10-27 (UTC+8).

  • vLLM: installation (NVIDIA CUDA), serving LoRA adapters, serve command reference, security guide.
  • uv: installation.
  • Licenses: Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 model card, Llama 3.2 Community License, Gemma Terms of Use.
  • DeepSeek: Terms of Use (Last Update: March 27, 2026).
  • CloudGPU: terms, acceptable use policy, privacy policy, docs, pricing.

Step 2: rent a raw GPU

On Deploy, choose Raw GPU and a card. The CloudGPU docs say that every template is a ready-made image with root SSH and that for anything a template does not cover you rent a raw GPU (Deploy â†’ Raw GPU) and install what you need over SSH. The docs' GPU table lists 16 GB as the minimum VRAM for models from 0.5B to 8B parameters; vLLM also needs Linux and an NVIDIA GPU with compute capability 7.5 or higher, according to its installation page. A 7B model in 16-bit needs memory for the weights plus a cache for requests, so a card with more than the minimum is the easy fix if the server reports it cannot fit.

Connect with the SSH details of your running instance. If you have an adapter, upload its folder from your own machine (scp takes the port with a capital -P):

scp -r -P  ./adapter-selfloop @:/workspace/

What to check: ssh -p @ connects, nvidia-smi lists a GPU, and (with an adapter) ls /workspace/adapter-selfloop shows adapter_config.json and adapter_model.safetensors.

Step 3: install vLLM in a fresh environment

pip install uv

uv venv --python 3.12 --seed --managed-python
source .venv/bin/activate
uv pip install vllm --torch-backend=auto

These lines follow the vLLM page as read on 2026-10-27; if the page now shows different commands, use its commands.

What to check: with the environment active, vllm --version prints a version, and python3 -c "import torch; print(torch.cuda.is_available())" prints True. If the install stops with an error, read the error text and the troubleshooting parts of the vLLM page.

Step 4: start the server on localhost, with your key

cd /workspace && source .venv/bin/activate
nohup vllm serve mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8000 \
  --api-key  \
  --tokenizer-mode hf \
  --enable-lora --max-lora-rank 16 \
  --lora-modules selfloop=/workspace/adapter-selfloop \
  > /workspace/vllm.log 2>&1 &

Without an adapter, remove the --enable-lora, --max-lora-rank and --lora-modules lines.

What the flags do, from the vLLM serve reference and LoRA page: --host 127.0.0.1 keeps the HTTP server on the instance's localhost; --api-key makes requests under /v1 carry that key; --tokenizer-mode hf uses the Hugging Face tokenizer instead of letting auto pick the mistral_common tokenizer for Mistral models; pinning it is meant to match how an adapter was trained with the Hugging Face tokenizer, so drop the flag if your adapter was trained another way; --lora-modules name=path registers the adapter under the name selfloop; --max-lora-rank must be at least the adapter's r and the docs list the allowed values (the default is 16), so if your r from Step 1 is larger than 16, use the next allowed value. The key is visible in the instance's process list while the server runs, which is one more reason to use a fresh key per instance.

Wait until the log says the server is ready before you send a request. If the process exits, read the end of the log with tail -n 50 /workspace/vllm.log. A message about memory for the cache is fixed by adding --max-model-len 8192 or by choosing a card with more memory.

Step 5: open the tunnel and call your endpoint (on your own machine)

ssh -N -L 8000:127.0.0.1:8000 -p  @

import os
import sys

BASE = "mistralai/Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3"
ADAPTER = "selfloop"  # delete this name from the loop below if you started without an adapter

question = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "Explain what a LoRA adapter is in two sentences."

for name in (BASE, ADAPTER):
    reply = client.chat.completions.create(
        model=name,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}],
        temperature=0,
        max_tokens=300,
    )
    print("==", name)
    print(reply.choices[0].message.content)
    print()

Run it with the key in an environment variable, not in the file:

python3 ask.py "Explain what a LoRA adapter is in two sentences."

Any tool that lets you set an OpenAI-compatible base URL and a key can use the same two values (http://127.0.0.1:8000/v1 and your key) while the tunnel is open.

What to check: the curl call lists the model names you expect; ask.py prints one answer per model name; and a call with a wrong or missing key is refused rather than answered. If the tunnel command prints "address already in use", use another local port. Reading two answers is not a test of your adapter; for that, use questions the adapter never saw and compare them yourself, as in the self-critique guide.

Step 6: stop, copy out what you need, destroy

Close the tunnel with Ctrl+C in its terminal. Before you destroy anything, copy what you want to keep. The docs have a section called "What to save before you destroy an instance"; read it in the CloudGPU docs. For example, copy the server log from your own machine:

scp -P  @:/workspace/vllm.log ./

Then destroy the instance from your Dashboard (the docs: "You can destroy an instance at any time"). Minutes spent copying are billed like any other minute, and billing stops once the instance is destroyed. The endpoint key was meant for this instance only; do not reuse it.

What to check: the instance no longer appears as running in your Dashboard, and the curl call from Step 5 now fails to connect.

Privacy and access, in plain terms

  • This is your own endpoint, with your own API key, reached through your own SSH tunnel. It is not a public URL.
  • Per CloudGPU's terms (section 5), you keep ownership of any data, models, code or output you create on or upload to an instance, and CloudGPU says it does not access, inspect, copy or back up the contents of your instance except in three listed cases: a credible report of a violation of section 3, valid legal process, or to protect the safety of users or third parties.
  • Per the same terms, destroying an instance permanently deletes its local storage, and you are responsible for backing up what you want to keep.
  • Whatever you send to the endpoint is processed on that rented instance. Do not send secrets or personal data you would not put on a rented machine.
  • If you call a model through CloudGPU's AI API instead of your own instance, the request is forwarded to the model provider and its terms apply; see the privacy policy.

Sources

All read on 2026-10-27 (UTC+8).

  • uv: installation.
  • Licenses: Mistral 7B Instruct v0.3 model card, Llama 3.2 Community License, Gemma Terms of Use.
  • DeepSeek: Terms of Use (Last Update: March 27, 2026).
  • CloudGPU: terms, acceptable use policy, privacy policy, docs, pricing.

title: What cron expression runs every 5 minutes?
summary:
A cleanup job was supposed to run every five minutes. The crontab was saved at 10:03. The log showed 10:05, then 10:10. That is not a late start. The expression is tied to the clock, at minutes 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, and 55. Saving the file does not start a countdown. Classic cron also does not hold the next start while the previous process is still running, so a six-minute command overlaps itself. What follows is the five-field form used by Vixie cron and cronie, not a systemd timer and not Quartz.

Five fields, then the command

A standard line is five time fields and then the command. None of them is a seconds field.

Field Range A star means
Minute 0–59 Every minute
Hour 0–23 Every hour
Day of month 1–31 Every day of the month
Month 1–12 Every month
Day of week 0–7 Every day of the week

On Vixie cron and on cronie, Sunday is both 0 and 7. Monday is 1 and Friday is 5, so 1-5 is Monday through Friday. Some other schedulers accept only 0 for Sunday. Read crontab(5) on the host before using 7. Prefer numbers to names such as MON or JAN.

The fields use the daemon’s timezone, so 0 0 * * * is midnight there, not necessarily UTC. Honor CRON_TZ only if that host’s crontab(5) says so.

Every 5, 10, 15, and 30 minutes

Each line below is aligned to the clock, and each one includes minute 0.

*/5 * * * *     # 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55
*/10 * * * *    # 0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50
*/15 * * * *    # 0, 15, 30, 45
*/30 * * * *    # 0 and 30

The edit time is not stored. A line installed at 10:03 still waits for 10:05, then 10:10.

5-59/5 * * * * starts the range at 5, so minute 0 is left out. Use it only when you mean to skip the top of the hour. For a plain every-five-minutes job, keep */5 * * * *.

Drop the step when you want an hour or a day instead.

0 * * * *       # every hour, at minute 0
0 0 * * *       # every day at 00:00
0 9 * * *       # every day at 09:00
0 9 * * 1-5     # Monday through Friday at 09:00

0 * * * * fires 24 times a day, 0 0 * * * once at midnight, and 0 9 * * 1-5 on weekdays at 09:00 because day-of-month stays a star. The either-day rule starts only when both day fields are restricted. A day field that starts with *, including */2, is not restricted. See why cron runs on the wrong day.

How a step is counted

A step is a range plus /n. In the minute field, * means 0-59, so */5 is 0, then every fifth minute through 55. Twelve runs an hour.

In the hour field, 0 */2 * * * is minute 0 of every second hour: 00:00, 02:00, 04:00, and so on through 22:00.

Day of month starts at 1, not 0. On Vixie cron and cronie, * in that field is 1-31, so 0 0 */5 * * is midnight on the 1st, 6th, 11th, 16th, 21st, 26th, and 31st. It is not the dates divisible by 5 (the 5th, 10th, 15th, 20th, 25th, and 30th). If the daemon is not cronie, test that list. A cron expression generator shows the five fields. It does not simulate one daemon’s calendar, and it does not install the job.

Mistakes that move the run

Copy the five fields, not the sentence beside them. Crontab does not read “every five minutes.”

Do not add a seconds field in front. The other fields shift right. Quartz uses six fields, or seven with a year, and seconds come first. Spring uses that six-field form. EventBridge’s six fields are minutes, hours, day-of-month, month, day-of-week, and year, with no seconds field. Quartz and EventBridge both use ? in a day field. A five-field line matches neither shape.

Traditional Vixie cron does not skip a run because the previous process is still going. If the work must not overlap, take a lock in the command, for example with flock, and leave the schedule alone. systemd timers and queue workers can differ. This warning is about classic cron.

Cron’s PATH is often shorter than a login shell. Call the program by its absolute path. A stored “next run” in an API is often a Unix timestamp, not an expression. Read that number on the Unix timestamp converter. Do not paste it into the minute field.

*/5 cannot mean “five minutes from now.” Sleep in a process, or use a queue delay. The daemon still starts the command once, when the minute begins, not again at second 10 or 20.

Try it for one cycle

Point a throwaway line at a file you can delete.

*/5 * * * * date >> /tmp/cron-every-5.log

Wait until two lines are written. The minutes should be five apart, and each minute should be divisible by 5. Then delete the line. Some hosts log the start with journalctl -u cron. Others still use syslog. Use the log that machine keeps.

Full guide with the FAQ and a cron generator: https://kepttools.com/guides/cron-every-5-minutes

title: Black October: 9 AI Dev Platforms Were Breached. Rotate Your Keys Today
summary:
TL;DR: In October 2026, at least nine AI developer platforms disclosed security incidents, according to a Wiz research post published on October 30. The common thread is that attackers went after stored environment variables, especially the ones that unlock AI models. Stolen keys were tested within about 30 minutes and later resold. If you have an OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock or similar key sitting in a hosting or dev platform, rotate it today. Then put a spend cap on it and narrow its scope. There's a checklist below.

Any other month, one AI platform breach would have been the security story of the week. This month there were nine, and Wiz's researchers had to point out that hardly anyone was connecting them. They called it "Black October".

I'm writing this for developers and small teams, not security specialists. Most of us have pasted an LLM API key into a platform dashboard at some point because it was the quickest way to get a demo running. This post covers what's confirmed so far, what attackers did with the keys, and what you can do in the next hour.

The nine incidents, as Wiz lists them

This is Wiz's list with the disclosure dates they give:

Date (Oct 2026) Platform
Oct 6 Fireworks AI
Oct 9 Andromeda
Oct 14 Zeabur
Oct 15 Lightning AI
Oct 16–17 OpenCode
Oct 20 Railway
Oct 23 Warp
Oct 28 CommandCode
Oct 30 Northflank

What's known about each one varies a lot. Most of these incidents are still under investigation, and Wiz says detailed technical information mostly isn't public yet. Here's what the post does say, attributed to the companies:

  • Fireworks, OpenCode and Warp reported signs of an "agent swarm" attack. Andromeda called its incident part of an "industry-wide attack."
  • OpenCode and CommandCode explicitly attributed their incidents to an attempt at "distillation" (using stolen model access to train or copy models).
  • Fireworks, Zeabur and Lightning AI attribute their root causes to credential access. Wiz notes that Lightning AI had previously been hit by a supply chain attack in the Mini-Shai Hulud campaign.
  • Railway has released a preliminary report and says it believes initial access came through "privilege escalation in our build infrastructure."
  • Warp has suggested the root cause was a third-party vendor dependency, and OpenCode points to a "legacy system."
  • Zeabur has published a full write-up and, according to Wiz, will shut down because of the incident.

There's no single shared vulnerability. Wiz says no single vulnerability or dependency links these attacks. The shared pattern is what the attackers wanted: every public report describes targeted hunting for stored environment variables, with a focus on those that grant AI access.

Unconfirmed: whether one group is behind all nine incidents. Wiz doesn't claim that, and neither do I.

Why your AI key is now worth stealing

Wiz ties the campaign to two trends. Agentic attacks let attackers compromise targets faster. LLMJacking is the other: stolen model access gets resold through "LLM broker" services. The resale market is what turns a stolen key into money quickly, and that's why so many people are now hunting for these keys.

Wiz also traced downstream abuse of two enterprise keys, which it could attribute to one of the vendor breaches. Both cases are worth reading in full. These are the numbers that matter for your own setup:

  • Validation came fast. In both cases, the first unauthorised call came within 30 minutes of the reported credential access at the vendor. It was a single model call from a residential IP, made during a one-minute sweep that tested stolen keys across multiple organisations.
  • Case A (unrestricted key): Over about 30 hours, until the key was remediated, the actor made approximately 800,000 Bedrock calls, about 90% of them successful. The key's policy allowed global.* cross-region inference profiles, which spread the load across regions, so only about 6% of calls were throttled.
  • Case B (restricted key): This key only allowed Bedrock through us.* inference profiles. The reseller pool asked for global.*, so thousands of calls failed at first. Then a checker found the working us.* model IDs, and over about 13 hours a single address made approximately 1.7 million calls, over a million of them successful. Most of the rest were throttled by the account's regional quotas.
  • The cost: At list price, Wiz estimates these two cases alone likely ran up over $100k in usage.

Case B doesn't show that restrictions save you. They didn't stop the abuse. They slowed it, and the regional quotas limited it. That's the right way to think about scoping: it limits how much damage a stolen key can do, and you still have to rotate fast.

Wiz also mentions anecdotal impact reports from social media: alleged theft of about $371,000 in cryptocurrency using crypto keys stored in Railway, and stolen AI access (for example from OpenCode) producing consumer bills in the hundreds to thousands of dollars. Treat these as reports, not confirmed totals.

Northflank's advice is the right default for everyone

Northflank, the most recent platform on the list, put out the clearest customer guidance I've seen this month. Its status page told every customer to assume all environment variables have been decrypted and to rotate everything: secrets on workloads, secret groups and global secrets. It also recommended disabling public access to database addons, and said multiple users had confirmed their AI keys had been used. A later update told customers to revoke credentials with the issuing provider (not just change them in Northflank) and to check AI provider usage and billing logs for unexpected activity.

You don't have to be a Northflank customer for this to apply. If a platform that stores your env vars discloses an incident, the safe assumption is that every value in those env vars is gone. You rotate the keys first and investigate later.

The rotation checklist (do this today)

Start with every platform that holds an AI key: hosting, CI, notebook services, agent platforms and coding tools.

  1. Make the inventory. List every AI key (OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock/IAM, Google, Mistral, OpenRouter and so on), and note which platform and which environment holds it. If you can't say where a key lives, assume it's on one of these platforms.
  2. Create the replacement first. Generate a new key at the provider, update the platform secret and redeploy. Confirm the app works.
  3. Revoke the old key at the provider. Deleting it from the platform isn't enough, because the attacker has a copy. Revocation has to happen where the key was issued.
  4. Do the non-AI secrets too. Database URLs, payment keys, cloud credentials, webhook signing secrets and crypto wallet keys. Northflank's "rotate everything" applies here, and the Railway reports show attackers take whatever they find.
  5. Read your usage and billing logs. Look for unfamiliar models, regions or IPs, traffic at odd hours, or a sudden jump in output tokens. In Wiz's cases there was only a trickle of validation calls for days before the flood, so a small amount of strange usage still matters.
  6. Report abuse. Tell the provider and the platform. Some providers can help with fraudulent usage if you report it quickly.
  7. Write down the date. Add each rotation to your secrets inventory, so the next incident takes ten minutes, not an afternoon.

Spend caps and scoped keys: treat AI keys like payment cards

A stolen AI key works like a payment card with no limit. So put a limit on it.

  • Set the hardest spend limit your provider offers. Most AI provider consoles have per-project or per-workspace budgets, limits or alerts. A hard limit is better than an alert, and an alert that wakes someone up beats a monthly invoice. Set it close to your real usage, not 10x above it.
  • One key per app, per environment. Production, staging and that weekend prototype shouldn't share a key. When one leaks, you rotate one key and you can see exactly whose usage it was.
  • Restrict models and regions. On Bedrock, use IAM policies that allow only the specific models and inference profiles your app calls. Case B shows the effect: abuse was delayed and capped by regional quotas instead of spreading worldwide.
  • Use short-lived credentials where you can. Workload identity or OIDC role assumption for cloud model access means there's no long-lived key in an env var to steal.
  • Keep keys out of the platform where possible. If a platform supports pulling secrets from a dedicated secrets manager at runtime, use that, so the platform holds a reference instead of the value.

What we do on our projects

On our own client projects we keep production AI keys in the cloud provider's secrets manager rather than pasting them into every dashboard. Each environment gets its own key, and each provider account gets a budget alert. When a platform we use discloses an incident, we rotate first and investigate second. This month, the habit that made the biggest difference was keeping a written list of where every key lives. Rotating takes minutes. Working out where the keys are is the slow part.

What's still unknown

  • Whether the incidents share an operator. Wiz links resale infrastructure to keys from at least one breach, but says it can't definitively tie the resellers to the initial compromises.
  • Root causes for most of the nine platforms. Only Zeabur has a full write-up and Railway a preliminary report, according to Wiz.
  • How many customer keys were taken in total. No platform has published that number yet.

I'll update this post if the platforms publish more detailed reports.

Where does your AI API key live right now?

Be honest: how many dashboards hold a copy of your OpenAI or Anthropic key at the moment? Have you set a spend limit on any of them? Tell me in the comments. I'm curious whether this month has changed how anyone stores these keys.

Wiz also traced downstream abuse of two enterprise keys, which it could attribute to one of the vendor breaches. Both cases are worth reading in full. These are the numbers that matter for your own setup:

The rotation checklist (do this today)

  • Keep keys out of the platform where possible. If a platform supports pulling secrets from a dedicated secrets manager at runtime, use that, so the platform holds a reference instead of the value.

What we do on our projects

On our own client projects we keep production AI keys in the cloud provider's secrets manager rather than pasting them into every dashboard. What's still unknown

  • Whether the incidents share an operator. Wiz links resale infrastructure to keys from at least one breach, but says it can't definitively tie the resellers to the initial compromises.
  • Root causes for most of the nine platforms. Only Zeabur has a full write-up and Railway a preliminary report, according to Wiz.
  • How many customer keys were taken in total. No platform has published that number yet.

I'll update this post if the platforms publish more detailed reports.

Where does your AI API key live right now?

Be honest: how many dashboards hold a copy of your OpenAI or Anthropic key at the moment? Have you set a spend limit on any of them? Tell me in the comments. I'm curious whether this month has changed how anyone stores these keys.

title: Stop Debugging Services That Never Ran: Practical systemd Conditions and Asserts on Linux
summary:
You enable a unit, start it, and get... nothing. No error. systemctl start exits 0. systemctl status says inactive (dead). There is no traceback, no failed state, no red text — just a service that quietly declined to exist.

Nine times out of ten that is not a broken unit file. It is a Condition...= line doing exactly what it was told, and systemd skipping the start silently.

Conditions are one of the least documented and most useful parts of unit files. They let a single image boot on a laptop and a server, let a backup job refuse to run when the backup disk is not mounted, and let a provisioning unit run exactly once. Used carelessly, they produce the invisible-service problem above.

Everything below was checked against systemd 257.13 on Debian 13, with the observed output quoted verbatim.

Conditions are checked at job execution time, not at enable time

A condition is not a dependency and not an install-time guard. It is evaluated at the moment the queued start job is about to run — after the units ordered before it have finished. That timing matters: a condition can test state that After= dependencies just produced.

The semantics, from systemd.unit(5):

  • Multiple conditions are ANDed. All must hold.
  • A leading ! negates a single condition.
  • A leading | turns a condition into a triggering condition: if any triggering condition holds, and all non-triggering conditions hold, the unit starts. The order is |! — pipe first, exclamation second.
  • Assigning the empty string (ConditionPathExists=) resets the entire condition list.
  • All path checks follow symlinks, except ConditionPathIsSymbolicLink=.

If a condition fails, systemd skips the start "mostly silently". The unit does not enter failed. Ordering is still honoured, and dependent units are pulled in as if the unit had activated — the skip happens at the last moment.

Conditions versus asserts: the difference you can observe

Asserts are the loud twin. Same argument syntax, prefixed Assert..., but an unmet assert fails the job, not the unit.

I wrote two throwaway units to confirm the behaviour on systemd 257. One had ConditionPathExists=/nonexistent/lyra-marker, the other AssertPathExists=/nonexistent/lyra-marker. Results:

# condition unit
$ systemctl start lyra-condtest.service
$ echo $?
0
$ systemctl status lyra-condtest.service
○ lyra-condtest.service - Lyra condition test
     Loaded: loaded (/run/systemd/system/lyra-condtest.service; static)
     Active: inactive (dead)

# assert unit
$ systemctl start lyra-asserttest.service
Assertion failed on job for lyra-asserttest.service.
$ echo $?
1

The journal tells the real story:

lyra-condtest.service - Lyra condition test skipped, unmet condition check ConditionPathExists=/nonexistent/lyra-marker
lyra-asserttest.service: Starting requested but asserts failed.
Assertion failed for lyra-asserttest.service - Lyra condition test.

So: conditions skip quietly and succeed; asserts fail loudly and exit non-zero. Neither one moves the unit into failed. That last point surprises people — an assert does not set the unit's failed state, it only fails the queued job, so systemctl is-failed still reports inactive. If your monitoring only looks at unit state, you can miss an assertion failure entirely.

The rule of thumb: use a condition when the unit genuinely does not apply to this machine (wrong architecture, no battery, already provisioned). Use an assert when the unit absolutely should run but something the administrator must fix is wrong.

The conditions that earn their keep

There are around thirty conditions. These are the ones that solve real problems.

Hardware and platform

  • ConditionArchitecture= — x86-64, arm64, native; valued on mixed-architecture fleets sharing one image.
  • ConditionVirtualization= — vm, container, or a specific engine: kvm, docker, podman, systemd-nspawn, private-users. ConditionVirtualization=!container is the standard way to keep a unit off containers.
  • ConditionCPUFeature= (v248) — x86 and arm64 feature checks, e.g. avx2 or arm64.bti.
  • ConditionSecurity= — selinux, apparmor, ima, audit, uefi-secureboot, tpm2. Useful for units that only make sense with a given LSM active.
  • ConditionACPower= — true holds if at least one AC connector is connected or if no AC connector is known at all. That fallback keeps server units working; it also means the condition passes on machines that cannot report power state.
  • ConditionCapability= — checks a capability in the manager's bounding set, not the service's effective set.

Runtime environment

  • ConditionPathExists= and friends — !path negation, ConditionPathExistsGlob=, ConditionPathIsDirectory=, ConditionPathIsMountPoint=, ConditionPathIsReadWrite=, ConditionPathIsSymbolicLink=, ConditionDirectoryNotEmpty=, ConditionFileNotEmpty=, ConditionFileIsExecutable=.
  • ConditionPathIsEncrypted= (v246) — true only when the backing block device is dm-crypt/LUKS. It does not detect ext4 per-directory encryption, and it does not look through loopback devices.
  • ConditionKernelCommandLine= — matches a word or an exact key=value from /proc/cmdline. Read from /proc/1/cmdline when systemd runs as a container payload, which is a nice detail when your condition behaves differently in a container.
  • ConditionFirstBoot= and ConditionNeedsUpdate= — image provisioning primitives.
  • ConditionUser= / ConditionGroup= — mainly for user managers. ConditionUser=@system matches the system UID range, and is pointless for the system manager, which always runs as root.

Lab 1: a maintenance switch that actually stops work

The highest-value pattern in the whole set is a negated path check used as an operator kill switch.

# /etc/systemd/system/nightly-backup.service
[Unit]
Description=Nightly restic backup to /srv/backup
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target

# Operator pause switch: touch this file and this unit will not run.
ConditionPathExists=!/etc/backup/pause

# Refuse to run unless the backup target is actually mounted.
ConditionPathIsMountPoint=/srv/backup

# If the config is missing, fail loudly instead of silently doing nothing.
AssertPathExists=/etc/restic/password

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/backup.sh

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo touch /etc/backup/pause
sudo systemctl start nightly-backup.service   # exits 0, does nothing
sudo journalctl -u nightly-backup.service -b --no-pager | tail -2
# ... skipped, unmet condition check ConditionPathExists=!/etc/backup/pause
sudo rm /etc/backup/pause

Two things worth noticing. The condition is re-evaluated on every start attempt, so it also gates timer-driven activations. And it is not a watchdog: nothing re-checks the file until something starts the unit again.

If you pair this with systemd.timer, put the condition on the service, not the timer. A condition on the timer prevents the timer from starting at all; a condition on the service is evaluated at each activation, which is what you usually want for a pause switch.

Lab 2: only back up on AC power

A laptop that starts a three-hour rsync at 20% battery is a design bug.

# ~/.config/systemd/user/laptop-sync.service
[Unit]
Description=Sync home directory to NAS
ConditionACPower=true
After=network-online.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=%h/bin/sync-home.sh

Test it without unplugging anything:

systemd-analyze condition --unit=laptop-sync.service
echo $?    # 0 = would start, 1 = would be skipped

Vendor units sometimes assert paths you do not have. Resetting an assert requires clearing the list first, because AssertPathExists= is a list setting:

# /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service.d/10-local-paths.conf
[Unit]
# Clear every inherited assertion of this name, then re-add ours.
AssertPathExists=
AssertPathExists=/etc/myapp/config.toml
AssertDirectoryNotEmpty=/var/lib/myapp

Without the empty assignment you would end up with both the vendor's path and yours, and the unit would fail the job for a path that is irrelevant on this host.

This is also the correct place for "the database directory must exist before we start", because a missing directory is an operator problem, not a reason to silently skip.

Lab 4: run provisioning exactly once

First boot semantics are built in: ConditionFirstBoot=yes is true while /etc was unpopulated at boot, and it stops being true once the manager finishes its startup phase.

# /etc/systemd/system/site-provision.service
[Unit]
Description=One-time site provisioning
ConditionFirstBoot=yes
Wants=first-boot-complete.target
Before=first-boot-complete.target

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/local/sbin/provision.sh
RemainAfterExit=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

The Wants= plus Before= pairing is the part people skip. first-boot-complete.target is what marks first boot as done; ordering the provisioning unit before it means an aborted first boot re-runs the unit next time instead of leaving a half-configured system.

ConditionNeedsUpdate=/etc solves the neighbouring problem — running a migration only when /usr is newer than the .updated stamp file. Units using it should order themselves before systemd-update-done.service, which resets that stamp.

Debugging a unit that will not start

Work in this order. Every command below is read-only.

# 1. What did systemd decide, and why?
systemctl show myapp.service -p ActiveState -p ConditionResult -p AssertResult
# ActiveState=inactive
# ConditionResult=no
# AssertResult=yes

# 2. Which condition failed? (works without starting anything)
systemd-analyze condition --unit=myapp.service
# myapp.service: ConditionPathIsMountPoint=/srv/backup failed.
# Conditions failed.

# 3. The journal has the human-readable reason.
journalctl -u myapp.service -b --no-pager | grep -i -e condition -e assert

Two practical notes from actually running these:

  • systemctl show -p Conditions prints Conditions=[unprintable] because it is a structured property. Use ConditionResult for the verdict and systemd-analyze condition for the detail.
  • systemd-analyze condition also accepts bare expressions, which is handy for testing syntax before you commit a unit: systemd-analyze condition 'ConditionPathExists=/etc/passwd' prints a per-condition pass/fail line and exits 1 if the set fails.

And the trap that started this article: systemctl start exits 0 when a condition skips a unit. Any deploy script that checks only the exit code will happily report success while the service never ran.

Where conditions go wrong

  • They are not dependency control. The man page is explicit: conditions are evaluated long after jobs are queued, so they are "not suitable for conditionalizing unit dependencies". If B must not run without A, use Requires=/After=, not a condition on B.
  • Nothing re-evaluates them spontaneously. A condition that becomes true later does not start the unit. Use a .path unit or a timer to create the start job.
  • They do not interact with Restart=. A skipped unit never started, so there is no restart to perform. A unit whose condition starts failing on a later start will just stop, cleanly.
  • Broken symlinks fail ConditionPathExists= because path checks resolve symlinks. Use ConditionPathIsSymbolicLink= to test the link itself.
  • ConditionKernelVersion= is unportable. Distributions backport features into older version strings, so a version number does not tell you what the kernel supports. The man page calls this out directly.
  • systemd-analyze verify does not evaluate conditions. It catches unit syntax and missing executables, not whether a condition will pass on this host.

The short version

A unit that will not start and will not explain itself is almost always a condition. Check ConditionResult, run systemd-analyze condition --unit=, read the journal line, and the mystery collapses in about ten seconds.

Use conditions for "this unit does not belong here", asserts for "this host is misconfigured and someone should know", and never for dependency logic. The negated path check alone — ConditionPathExists=!/etc/service/pause — is worth adding to every scheduled job you own.

References

  • systemd.unit(5), Conditions and Asserts: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd.unit.html
  • systemd-analyze(1), condition verb: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd-analyze.html
  • systemctl(1): https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemctl.html
  • systemd-detect-virt(1) for the virtualization identifiers accepted by ConditionVirtualization=
  • machine-id(5), First Boot Semantics: https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/machine-id.html
  • systemd.special(7) for first-boot-complete.target

title: OpenDsec: self-hosted sandboxes for RL rollouts and code-running agents
summary:
If you train a model with agentic reinforcement learning, every rollout needs somewhere to run code: install a package, run the tests, hit the network, write files. Thousands of those run at once. When the training job is preempted they all have to stop together and come back later. And when you want to explore one state several ways, you want copies of the environment as it is right now, memory included, not fresh ones from the image.

Hosted sandbox services cover part of this. We wanted all of it on our own machines, so we built OpenDsec and published it under the AGPL.

This is the first post in a series about it. Here: what it does, what it looks like to run, and where its limits are.

One run, start to finish

That is a real recording on one bare-metal server: the install script, then a short Python program that creates a Firecracker microVM, runs print(6*7) in it and forks it into four copies. The six minutes of building and installing are cut; everything after runs at real speed. The 0.16 s is the whole API call (placement, boot, the in-VM agent ready), measured from the client.

The program is the whole client side:

import asyncio, time
from opendsec import DSecClient, DSecRunArgs

async def main():
    async with DSecClient() as client:
        t = time.perf_counter()
        sb = await client.run_sandbox(DSecRunArgs(backend="microvm", image="root/py:3.12"))
        print(f"ready in {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s (whole API call: placement + boot)")
        print((await sb.run_shell("python3 -c 'print(6*7)'")).stdout.strip())
        t = time.perf_counter()
        forks = await sb.fork(count=4)    # copies with memory
        print(f"forked 4 in {time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")
        await asyncio.gather(*(s.stop() for s in [sb, *forks]))

asyncio.run(main())

Where the design comes from

DeepSeek described the sandbox platform behind their agentic RL training in DeepSeek Elastic Compute (DSec). OpenDsec follows that paper: a stateless apiserver, IAM with nested projects and quotas, a watcher that aggregates scheduling state, power-of-k placement where each node has the final say on admission, layered images loaded on demand, a default-deny network policy, and pausing a whole task at once.

Where the paper leaves things open, or where we chose differently, the decisions are ours: nftables and a DNS proxy instead of eBPF for the network policy, any shared file system (NFS, CephFS, JuiceFS) instead of 3FS for images, and Firecracker with memory snapshots as the main backend. The design document marks every point as either from the paper or our own.

OpenDsec is an independent project. It is not affiliated with DeepSeek and contains none of its code.

What you get

  • Three kinds of sandbox behind one API: Firecracker microVMs, containers, and full QEMU VMs. Exec, files, processes, PTY and HTTP into the sandbox work the same on all of them.
  • Fast microVMs. About 0.1 s for the VM to boot, about 55 ms to create one from a memory snapshot, about 50 ms to resume one from a pause.
  • Fork with memory. fork(count=N) pauses the source for about 10 ms and gives you N copies with the same processes, imports and open ports. On one node the copies share memory pages; on another node they pull the snapshot from the source node directly.
  • Scale. One 384-thread node took a burst of 5120 microVMs in 37 s. A two-node cluster took 8192 containers in one burst with no failures.
  • Task-level pause. Pause every sandbox of a training task in one call, push their memory to swap, resume them later.
  • E2B compatible. Code written for E2B's SDKs runs against your own machines after changing three environment variables (E2B_API_URL, E2B_SANDBOX_URL, E2B_API_KEY). E2B's own Python and JS SDK checks pass.
  • Operable. mTLS between all components, a Raft-replicated IAM, Prometheus metrics and alerts, staged rollouts with automatic rollback, offline installs. Restarting or upgrading any component leaves running sandboxes alone.

All numbers are our own measurements on our bare-metal machines; the design document says how each was measured. Your hardware will give different ones. For example, the fork time depends on the file system under the sandbox state: 0.1 s on XFS, which copies memory files by reflink, and about 1 s on ext4, which has to copy them.

Try it on one machine

You need a Linux x86_64 machine with systemd and cgroup v2 (we test on Ubuntu 24.04). MicroVMs also need /dev/kvm, so use bare metal or a cloud VM with nested virtualization; without it you get containers only.

sudo -i
apt update && apt install -y make git python3-venv
curl -fsSL https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.3.linux-amd64.tar.gz | tar -C /usr/local -xz
git clone https://github.com/kernflux/opendsec && cd opendsec
deploy/quickstart.sh

The script checks the machine, builds everything, downloads Firecracker and the guest kernel (checked against pinned hashes), installs the components as systemd services with their own CA, imports python:3.12 from Docker Hub, and runs one container and one microVM as a check. Then:

python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install ./sdk/python
. /root/opendsec-ops/demo.env
.venv/bin/python sdk/python/examples/quickstart.py

deploy/quickstart.sh --uninstall removes all of it again.

What it is not (yet)

  • It is 0.x. Interfaces may change before 1.0.
  • We have only verified Ubuntu 24.04 hosts. Other distributions, real GPUs and multi-node Kubernetes are untested.
  • It is infrastructure you run. There is no hosted version.

License

The servers are AGPL-3.0. The Python SDK, the Go client and the API definitions are Apache-2.0, so programs that only call OpenDsec are not bound by the AGPL. A commercial license is available for closed modifications.

Next in this series

Firecracker, gVisor and containers compared for running AI-generated code: isolation, start time, memory and compatibility, with measurements.

The code is at github.com/Kernflux/opendsec, the docs at kernflux.github.io. Issues and questions are welcome there or in the comments.
